capture.final_message:
Split the conjunction.

- For the first component, apply Dirichlet’s theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions: \(q\ge1\), \((a,q)=1\), and \(a<q\) imply infinitely many primes \(p\equiv a\pmod q\).

- For the analytic component, use the classical zero-free region for \(\zeta\):
  \[
  \zeta(s)\ne0\qquad\text{when}\qquad
  \Re s\ge 1-\frac{c}{\log |\Im s|},\quad |\Im s|>3.
  \]
  Choose a fixed sufficiently small \(A\in(0,\tfrac12]\). Since \((\log |t|)^{-9}\) is much smaller than \((\log |t|)^{-1}\), the requested region
  \[
  \sigma\ge1-\frac{A}{(\log|t|)^9}
  \]
  lies safely inside that zero-free region. Then use the partial-fraction/Hadamard representation of the completed zeta function, or the standard logarithmic-derivative estimate in a zero-free neighborhood, to obtain
  \[
  \left|\frac{\zeta'(\sigma+it)}{\zeta(\sigma+it)}\right|
  \ll \log |t|.
  \]
  Enlarging the constant converts this stronger estimate into the required \(C(\log|t|)^9\) bound for \(|t|>3\).

The essential analytic point is zero-freeness: without it, \(\zeta'/\zeta\) has poles at zeros of \(\zeta\), so no uniform bound on the stated region is possible.
